```plato
//==
// # Finite elements
//
// A linear-elastic finite-element analysis, end to end: element stiffness from
// shape-function gradients, assembly into a global system, essential boundary
// conditions and loads, an iterative solve, and the strain / stress readings
// taken back off the answer. Types are in `finite-elements.types.plato`; the
// material record and the beam the 1D path analyses are in
// `engineering.types.plato`.
//
// Two decisions shape everything below, and they are the same decision seen
// twice.
//
// **The assembled matrix is a coordinate-list `SparseMatrix`.** Its stated
// invariant (`matrices.types.plato`) is that the value at a position is the SUM
// of the entries naming it, so concatenating two entry lists is matrix addition.
// Assembly is therefore a `FlatMap` over the elements and nothing else — no
// scatter pass, no accumulation, no ordering requirement, and no mutable global
// matrix. That is the representation a pure language actually wants, and it is
// why nothing here needs a hash map from (row, column) to slot.
//
// **The solve is a conjugate gradient.** It follows from the representation: a
// coordinate list has no random access — `ElementAt` on it is a scan of every
// entry — so any method that indexes the matrix, Gaussian elimination and
// Cholesky included, is quadratic per element read before it does any
// arithmetic. A Krylov method never indexes the matrix; it only ever multiplies
// by it, and that product is one sweep of the entries. Elimination would also
// need pivoting and fill-in, both of which mean rebuilding the storage.
//
// Sections, in order:
//  - System vectors
//  - Sparse system operations
//  - Boundary conditions as vectors
//  - The constrained conjugate gradient
//  - The isotropic element kernel
//  - The linear tetrahedron
//  - The linear triangle
//  - Solid analysis
//  - Plane analysis
//  - Recovering strain and stress
//  - Reading a solution
//  - Euler-Bernoulli beams

library FiniteElements
{
    //==
    // # System vectors
    //
    // A system vector is a plain `Array<Number>`, one entry per degree of
    // freedom. The four operations below are everything the conjugate gradient
    // needs; each is one `Zip` or one fold, so none of them is worth a type.

    // The dot product of two system vectors of the same length.
    SystemDot(a: Array<Number>, b: Array<Number>): Number
        => SumOf(a.Zip(b, (x, y) => x * y));

    // The component-wise difference of two system vectors.
    SystemSubtract(a: Array<Number>, b: Array<Number>): Array<Number>
        => a.Zip(b, (x, y) => x - y);

    // `a + b * t`, component-wise: the vector update a conjugate-gradient step
    // makes four times over.
    SystemAddScaled(a: Array<Number>, b: Array<Number>, t: Number): Array<Number>
        => a.Zip(b, (x, y) => x + y * t);

    // The component-wise product of two system vectors. This one function is
    // both the diagonal preconditioner and the projection onto the free degrees
    // of freedom, because both are diagonal operators.
    SystemProduct(a: Array<Number>, b: Array<Number>): Array<Number>
        => a.Zip(b, (x, y) => x * y);

    // The Euclidean norm of a system vector.
    SystemNorm(a: Array<Number>): Number
        => SystemDot(a, a).Sqrt;

    //==
    // # Sparse system operations
    //
    // The two things a conjugate gradient asks of the assembled matrix: multiply
    // by a vector, and report the diagonal. Both are a single sweep of the
    // coordinate list, and neither reads an element by position.
    //
    // These are the only places in this library that use an affine `Buffer`.
    // Scattering into indexed slots is what a builder is for, and the buffer
    // never escapes the function that allocates it.

    // A number buffer of `n` slots, every one written to `value`. `new
    // Buffer<T>(n)` leaves slot contents to the runtime, so every accumulator
    // below starts here rather than from a bare allocation.
    FilledNumbers(n: Integer, value: Number): Buffer<Number>
    {
        var slots = new Buffer<Number>(n);
        var i = 0;
        while (i < n)
        {
            slots = slots.Set(i, value);
            i = i + 1;
        }
        return slots;
    }

    // The buffer with `value` added into one slot. The slot leads and the buffer
    // follows because a function dispatching on a `unique` type is dropped from
    // the emitted C# (plato-416).
    AddAt(slot: Integer, into: Buffer<Number>, value: Number): Buffer<Number>
        => into.Set(slot, into.At(slot) + value);

    // The product of a coordinate-list matrix with a system vector: one sweep of
    // the entries, each scattering its contribution into the row it names. The
    // cost is the entry count, independent of how the entries are ordered and of
    // how many of them repeat a position.
    Multiply(m: SparseMatrix, x: Array<Number>): Array<Number>
    {
        var accumulated = FilledNumbers(m.NumRows, 0.0);
        var k = 0;
        while (k < m.Entries.Count)
        {
            var e = m.Entries[k];
            accumulated = e.Row.AddAt(accumulated, e.Value * x[e.Column]);
            k = k + 1;
        }
        return accumulated.Freeze();
    }

    // The Jacobi (diagonal) preconditioner: the reciprocal of each diagonal
    // entry, and 1 wherever the diagonal is zero. A zero diagonal is not a
    // defect here — it is exactly what a constrained degree of freedom looks
    // like once the projection below has removed it from the system, and leaving
    // its multiplier at 1 keeps it harmless.
    // (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preconditioner#Jacobi_(or_diagonal)_preconditioner)
    JacobiInverseDiagonal(m: SparseMatrix): Array<Number>
    {
        var diagonal = FilledNumbers(m.NumRows, 0.0);
        var k = 0;
        while (k < m.Entries.Count)
        {
            var e = m.Entries[k];
            if (e.IsDiagonal) { diagonal = e.Row.AddAt(diagonal, e.Value); }
            k = k + 1;
        }
        return diagonal.Freeze().Map(x => x == 0.0 ? 1.0 : 1.0 / x);
    }

    // A list of degree-of-freedom contributions summed into a dense load vector.
    // Contributions may repeat a degree of freedom; they add, which is what lets
    // every load type below be resolved independently and simply concatenated.
    ScatterLoads(contributions: Array<DofLoad>, dofCount: Integer): Array<Number>
    {
        var loads = FilledNumbers(dofCount, 0.0);
        var k = 0;
        while (k < contributions.Count)
        {
            loads = contributions[k].Dof.Value.AddAt(loads, contributions[k].Amount);
            k = k + 1;
        }
        return loads.Freeze();
    }
```
